items.direction: Narrate this as a high-energy, feel-good YouTube video counting down eight Egypt facts that sound fake but are real. The Narrator is THRILLED and grinning the whole time: an excited, fun friend who just found out these facts about Egypt and is bursting to tell you. Huge smile you can hear in every line, bright and upbeat, warm and natural like real excited conversation, never like reading a script. Wide, lively pitch movement; real amazement on every number and reveal; playful delighted laughter in the voice on the funny bits (the top of Egypt being technically in Asia, unions taking notes, the very very quiet neighbours, whales with tiny legs and toes, rebuilding a temple like a giant puzzle, the tiny excavator digging out a giant ship, Pizza Hut being closer to Cleopatra than the pyramid). 'We are hungry' is said like the striking workers, playful and a little dramatic. The Abu Simbel move ('cut the temples into more than a thousand blocks') builds up with disbelief. The opening bet is a cheeky, confident challenge with a grin, and so is the closing 'how many of these did you think were fake'. Punch the key words with energy. Pace quick and bouncy, about 170 words per minute, short crisp pauses; never flat, calm, sleepy, monotone or documentary-serious, and never shouty or fake. Accent: native General American English, neutral American accent from first word to last. VOICE IDENTITY: the same person and the same high energy from the first line to the last. Pronounce 'Sinai' as 'SY-nye', 'Ramesses' as 'RAM-uh-seez', 'Wadi Al-Hitan' as 'WAH-dee al-hee-TAHN', 'Abu Simbel' as 'AH-boo SIM-bel', 'Aswan' as 'ahs-WAHN', 'Tethys' as 'TEE-this', 'Suez' as 'soo-EZ', 'Ever Given' as 'EV-er GIV-en', 'Giza' as 'GEE-zuh', 'Cleopatra' as 'klee-oh-PAT-ruh', 'necropolis' as 'neh-KROP-uh-lis', 'Cairo' as 'KY-roh'. Read ONLY the text provided, word for word: stop right after the final sentence and never add, invent or continue with any words of your own. The text is given one sentence group per line: read every line in order, do not skip any line.
lines: I bet you a hundred dollars that at least one of these Egypt facts sounds completely fake to you.
A country where almost everyone lives on a thin green line.
Whales in the middle of the desert.
And a queen who lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids.
Every single one of them is real. Let's count down.
Fact number eight. Egypt is in two continents at the same time.
Most of Egypt sits in Africa. But look east, past the Suez Canal.
That triangle of land is the Sinai Peninsula, and it's in Asia.
So you can drive from Africa to Asia without ever leaving Egypt. Just cross the canal.
And here's the funny part. Egypt's highest mountain, Mount Catherine, is in Sinai. So the top of Egypt is technically in Asia.
And the most famous mountain there, Mount Sinai, is in Asia too.
Fact number seven. Egypt had the first recorded strike in history.
More than three thousand years ago, the workers who carved the tombs in the Valley of the Kings weren't paid their food rations.
So, around eleven fifty-seven BC, under Pharaoh Ramesses the Third, they put down their tools and walked out.
Their protest was written down by a scribe. Their complaint? We are hungry.
They marched out shouting it, and when officials showed up with guards, one striker threatened to damage the royal tombs if anyone touched them.
They staged a sit-in behind a temple, and in the end, they got their rations.
Unions, take notes. The ancient Egyptians got there first.
Fact number six. In Cairo, people live in a cemetery.
It's called the City of the Dead. A giant necropolis, kilometres long, that's more than a thousand years old.
And between the tombs, there are homes. Families. Shops. Even a post office.
Nobody knows the exact number, but estimates run from about one hundred eighty thousand to half a million people living among the graves.
Living in the tombs isn't even officially allowed. But some of these tombs are bigger and cleaner than apartments in the city, with courtyards and gardens.
Some families have been there for generations. For them, the neighbours just happen to be very, very quiet.
Fact number five. There are whales in the Egyptian desert.
About a hundred and fifty kilometres southwest of Cairo is Wadi Al-Hitan. The Valley of the Whales.
Lying in the sand are more than four hundred ancient whale skeletons.
Around forty million years ago, all of this was sea.
Egypt was underwater, part of an ancient ocean called the Tethys.
Some of these whales were nearly twenty metres long, with huge jaws full of sharp teeth.
And here's the twist. Some of these whales still had legs. Tiny back legs, with feet and toes.
It's one of the best places on Earth to see whales evolving from land animals into ocean giants. It's even a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Fact number four. Egypt moved an entire temple. Up a cliff.
This is Abu Simbel. Built for Ramesses the Second, more than three thousand years ago.
Four giant statues of the pharaoh, each about twenty metres tall, carved straight out of the cliff.
For centuries, the temple was almost completely buried in sand, until it was rediscovered in the eighteen hundreds.
In the nineteen sixties, Egypt built the Aswan High Dam, and the new lake was going to swallow the temples whole.
So engineers from around the world did something insane. They cut the temples into more than a thousand blocks.
Some of those blocks weighed up to thirty tons.
Then they rebuilt everything sixty-five metres higher and two hundred metres back from the river, like a giant puzzle.
It took four years and about forty million dollars.
More than fifty countries chipped in to pay for it.
And the ancient trick still works. Twice a year, the sunrise reaches deep into the temple and lights up the statues inside.
Fact number three. Almost everyone in Egypt lives on a tiny strip of land.
Egypt has more than one hundred million people.
But about ninety-five percent of them live in just five percent of the country.
Look at it from above. Egypt is almost all desert, except for this one green line.
Out here, the Sahara covers almost everything.
The Nile. Its valley and its delta.
Step a few kilometres away from the river, and the green just stops. Farmland on one side. Sand on the other.
At night, from space, the Nile lights up like a long glowing flower in the dark.
Fact number two. One ship blocked the world.
About twelve percent of all global trade passes through Egypt's Suez Canal.
In March twenty twenty-one, a giant container ship called the Ever Given got blown sideways by strong winds.
And it got stuck. Wedged across the whole canal.
For six days, nothing could pass.
Tugboats pulled. Diggers dug. The tide came and went. And the ship didn't move.
More than three hundred and sixty ships queued up, holding an estimated nine point six billion dollars of trade every single day.
That's roughly four hundred million dollars of trade stuck for every hour it sat there.
And the most famous picture from the rescue? A tiny excavator, trying to dig out a ship four hundred metres long.
Fact number one. Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around twenty-five sixty BC.
Cleopatra died in thirty BC. That's about two thousand five hundred years later.
The Moon landing was in nineteen sixty-nine. Only about two thousand years after her.
So to Cleopatra, the pyramids were already ancient history.
Even the first Pizza Hut, opened in nineteen fifty-eight, is closer in time to Cleopatra than she was to the pyramid.
And that pyramid? For more than three thousand eight hundred years, it was the tallest building humans had ever made.
Taller than anything in Rome. Anything in Greece. It only lost the title in the thirteen hundreds, to a cathedral in England.
It was covered in smooth white stone back then, shining in the sun. What we see today is just the core.
So, how many of these did you think were fake?
Tell me in the comments. And which country should we do next?
If you learned something new, hit subscribe, because next time, it's another country that sounds made up.
